problem: End-to-end image-to-control networks lack geometry/dynamics structure and generalize poorly to unseen environments, while predicting depth then planning is brittle because small depth errors cause collisions in tight spaces.
motivation: Cameras are cheap, but vision-based navigation must handle vehicle geometry and non-holonomic dynamics precisely in tight indoor spaces. Predicting a structured representation (Riemannian Motion Policies) that a classical controller can consume combines learning with model-based control and gives interpretable behavior.
key_idea: Train a ResNet-50-based network to predict per-control-point Riemannian Motion Policies (accelerations and metrics) from an RGB image, then solve the optimal vehicle control analytically using control-point Jacobians and the Ackermann kinematic model.
insight: Predicting RMPs generalizes better than predicting controls or depth because it encodes vehicle geometry and dynamics explicitly and is more concise and less noisy than depth. Table I on 5 holdout Gibson houses shows this: reached 75.5-93.7% for RMPs versus 47-68.5% for controls, with collisions far lower than the depth baseline. Predicted RMPs are also interpretable (metric isocontours) and can be augmented with extra RMPs without retraining.
method: Expert RMP controller: 12 control points on the vehicle bounding box; goal RMP (attractive, identity metric, front 3 points only) and obstacle RMPs (repulsive, metric w(d) f f^T) computed from a 240° laser scan; extra scaling and a head-point damping RMP stabilise wiggle.
Kinematic model incorporation: q̈ parameterised as [forward accel, steering velocity] via Ackermann model, so the analytic least-squares solve (Eq. 5) returns feasible controls, including backing up.

Neural RMP network: pretrained ResNet-50 image features plus FC extractors for velocity, angular velocity and goal; concatenated and fed to an FC regressor predicting one RMP (2D acceleration + 3 values of a symmetric 2x2 metric) per control point; a non-learned solver outputs the control.
Baselines with matched architecture: predict-depth (1D laser scan of 50 values then RMP solver) and predict-controls (direct regression of controls reusing the feature extractor).
Training: imitation from expert RMP in Gibson, 60k trajectories from 15 spaces, L2 loss, DAgger after first epoch, randomized velocity, waypoint and lighting.
Deployment: TensorRT on Jetson TX2, 50 fps inference, 25 fps full loop on a 1/10 RC car; finetuned on ~13k real hallway images labelled by the expert RMP from laser scans.

setting.backbone: ResNet-50 (ImageNet-pretrained) + FC regressor, fine-tuned/trained with imitation (DAgger)
setting.training_data: 60k expert RMP-controller trajectories from 15 Gibson indoor spaces (DAgger-augmented); ~13k real hallway images with laser-scan-derived expert labels for finetuning
setting.observation: monocular RGB (224x224, 120° rectified fisheye) plus velocity, angular velocity and goal point/waypoint
setting.action_space: continuous speed and steering (solved from predicted RMPs via Ackermann kinematics)
setting.privileged: Expert labels use laser scans at training time only; waypoints from A* shortest path (sim) or laser localization (real) given at test time

numbers.eval_set_note: 5 holdout Gibson environments, >200 trajectories each; space8 shown
numbers.extra: waypoint = furthest visible point on A* path
numbers.evidence: Table I, space8: Predicting RMPs 88.1% reached, 7.4% collision

numbers_note: Custom benchmark (5 Gibson holdout houses, not a standard benchmark); real-world results are qualitative trajectories only (Figs. 7, 9). Baselines and expert rows omitted.
results: On five holdout Gibson houses, the neural RMP agent gets 75.5-93.7% reached with 1.6-7.4% collision, close to the laser-based expert (59.2-97.9%) and far better than predicting depth (73.3-89.0% reached, up to 22.5% collision) and predicting controls (47.4-68.5% reached, up to 25.5% collision). On a real RC car, after brief finetuning, RMP and control agents both traverse a hallway, and only the RMP agent backs up to escape a wall-facing start in the obstacle test.
limitations: RMP controller is a purely local policy and can get stuck (e.g. goal behind a large concave obstacle), so it needs a higher-level planner for waypoints.
Sim-to-real domain gap requires real-data finetuning; the real evaluation is qualitative, in a simple hallway, with no quantitative real-world metrics.
Depends on hand-tuned expert RMP parameters and laser-scan expert labels; depth finetuning suffers from laser/image misalignment.
